```
title: Tests don't run in CI on macOS, Windows or Linux, and the CPU/GPU equivalence tests never run in CI (gap 9)
author: THEtheChad
body:
## Summary

`cargo test` runs in CI only on FreeBSD. Nothing runs the tests on macOS, Windows or Linux x64, the three platforms people install LightCraft on, so platform-specific breakage reaches `main` and stays there until someone builds on that platform by hand. The CPU/GPU equivalence tests, the guard that keeps the GPU twin matching the CPU reference, never run in CI on any platform: they skip when there is no GPU adapter, and the code refuses the software adapters CI runners have.

This is gap 9 in `docs/gaps.md` (beta blocker, 6–12 h). This issue proposes a fix that stays inside the current design and adds no new runner types.

## Evidence

- `.github/workflows/` has `freebsd.yml` (the only workflow that runs `cargo test`), `packaging-lint.yml`, `release.yml` and `windows-arm64.yml`. `release.yml` builds packages on macOS, Windows and Linux but runs no tests. `windows-arm64.yml` runs the CLI natively and has no `cargo test` job (its header comment explains why).
- #989: on 2026-10-11, `main` did not compile on macOS (`eframe::App::on_exit` called with one argument in the macOS-only quit path), and 12 tests failed there. Nothing in CI could have caught it. The follow-ups (#990, #997, #1003, #1007, #1018) are still open.
- `crates/gpu/tests/equivalence.rs:19-25`: `gpu()` prints `skipped: no GPU adapter` and the test passes. `fallback.rs`, `memory.rs`, `shutdown.rs` and `shutdown_first.rs` do the same.
- `crates/gpu/src/ctx.rs:299-302`: `Gpu::new` returns `Err` for `wgpu::DeviceType::Cpu` ("the CPU pipeline is faster"). That is the right call for the app. The side effect is that lavapipe (Linux) and WARP (Windows), the only adapters on GitHub's standard runners, are never used, so the equivalence suite has never run in CI.

## What a test run on the three platforms finds today

I ran the workflow below on my fork, on `main` at 76b53778. All runners were standard GitHub-hosted ones with a cold cache.

| | `main` alone | `main` + #990, #997, #1003, #1007, #1018 |

title: Develop edits invalidate every library-wide query and sidebar cache (30-130 ms per slider tick at 100k photos)
author: THEtheChad
body:
## Summary

Every catalog op bumps one counter, `Catalog::revision`, and every library-wide cache keys on it. A slider drag applies one `SetDevelop` op per tick, so each tick throws away the grid's query result and the sidebar's caches, and the next frame redoes them over the whole library. On a 100k-photo library that is 30–120 ms of UI-thread work per tick, against the 16 ms slider budget in `CLAUDE.md`, before any rendering.

Most of those views don't read develop state at all. A few do (Has Edits, Edit Date, Cropped, the size rules), so the fix has to know which is which; it can't just stop invalidating on develop ops.

## Evidence (main @ 76b53778)

**The op path.** `panels/edit.rs:17-42` (`apply_slider_out`) sends `develop.set` on every drag tick. Inside an interaction `Session::set_develop` calls `apply_silent` (`crates/engine/src/lib.rs:594`) with an `Op::SetDevelop` that also stamps a new `edited` time. That goes to `Catalog::apply`, which always runs `self.revision += 1` (`crates/catalog/src/lib.rs:483`).

**The grid query.** `Session::visible()` (`crates/engine/src/lib.rs:841-843`) keys its cache on `(catalog.revision, format!("{:?}|{:?}|{:?}|{:?}|{:?}", source, filter, sort, browse, library_folder))`:
- the `Debug` format allocates and formats the whole filter every call. The filmstrip calls `visible_cloned()` every frame (`panels/detail.rs:2135`, and again for neighbour prefetch at `:490`), so this runs every frame even when nothing changed;
- after any revision bump it reruns `catalog.query` over every photo: filter, then sort. The `FileName` sort lowercases both names inside the comparator (`query.rs:372`), so that is about 2·n·log n allocations. Then `arrange_stacks`. `source_total()` (`:915`) does a second full query with the same key.

**UI caches.** `Caches` in `crates/ui-egui/src/lib.rs:1459-1790` (folder tree, keyword tree, keyword chips/ticks/names, people, counts, person names, By Date tree, filter-bar values, keyword suggestions, album counts…

title: Proposal: per-component render cache versions instead of one RENDER_CACHE_VERSION
author: THEtheChad
body:
## Summary

Proposal for discussion. There's no PR with it, because this is a design decision for the maintainers.

`RENDER_CACHE_VERSION` (`crates/engine/src/media.rs:65`, now 61) is one number covering every rendered thumbnail and view render. It is part of every disk and memory cache key (`media.rs:1100`, `:1142`, `:1230`). The rule is "bump when the pipeline's output changes". In practice:

- **It changes about five times a day.** 59 commits on `main` changed the constant between 2026-09-30 and 2026-10-11. By task id: 21 `LR-IMP-FORMATS` (one decoder each), 10 `LR-PROF-CAMERACOLOR`, 4 each `LR-IMP-CAMERA-COVERAGE`, `LR-EDIT-OPTICS-PROFILE` and `LR-EDIT-LIGHT-HIGHLIGHTS`, and a handful of milestone commits (`git log origin/main -G'RENDER_CACHE_VERSION: u64 =' -- crates/engine/src/media.rs`).
- **Every bump throws away every user's whole render cache.** A fix to Canon CR3 quantization (`5a975d0d`) or Kodak DCS520C TIFFs (`ea777710`) re-renders every JPEG, NEF, ARW and HEIC thumbnail in every library on the next launch. That is a full-library decode and render: minutes to hours on big libraries, on battery, right after an update.
- **Parallel PRs collide on the number.** Every open PR that touches decoding or rendering edits the same line, so they conflict textually. Worse, two PRs can land with the same new number and silently share a version. Contributors coordinate by hand in comments ("`RENDER_CACHE_VERSION` goes to 43, which collides with #829's bump; whichever merges second takes 44" on #832; again on #915 and #829). #979 says "Invalidate old rendered previews (version 51)" while main is at 61.

## What is already versioned separately

- `camera_profiles::cache_key()` (`camera_profiles.rs:156`): changes with the profiles folder's contents.
- `camera_preview::LOOK_VERSION` (`camera_preview.rs:~22`): the camera-look fit, for smart-preview proxies.
- `DevelopSettings::process` (`docs/process-versions.md`): deliberate look changes ship as a new process, and the p…

title: Bug: Images are automatically saved to the library on every app launch
author: egsk4
body:
## Bug: Duplicate thumbnail images are created every time Lightcraft launches

### Description
Whenever I launch Lightcraft, the application automatically saves new copies of images to my local storage, even though I never manually saved or exported them.

The images appear in:

`C:\Users\USER\Pictures\LightCraft Library\thumbs`

Every time I reopen the application, new copies of the same images are created. These images also appear in Windows Gallery.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Launch Lightcraft.
2. Navigate to `C:\Users\USER\Pictures\LightCraft Library\thumbs`.
3. Close Lightcraft.
4. Launch Lightcraft again.
5. Check the folder and observe that new copies of the same images have been created.

### Expected Behavior
Lightcraft should reuse existing thumbnails or update them when necessary instead of creating duplicate copies every time the application launches.

### Actual Behavior
Lightcraft creates new copies of the same images on every launch, unnecessarily consuming SSD storage and causing duplicate images to appear in Windows Gallery.

### Impact
- Unnecessary disk space consumption over time.
- Duplicate images appearing in Windows Gallery.
- Potentially excessive disk writes on every application launch.

### Environment
- **OS:** Windows
- **Storage:** SSD
- **Affected directory:** `C:\Users\USER\Pictures\LightCraft Library\thumbs`

### Possible Cause
The thumbnail caching system may be regenerating thumbnails on every launch instead of checking for and reusing existing files.

title: 0.6.0: `run --import <folder>` skips HEIC/HEIF (the CLI's PHOTO_EXTENSIONS lags the engine's EXTENSIONS)
author: charles-hood
body:
**Environment:** lightcraft-cli 0.6.0, macOS universal zip, Apple silicon. This build decodes HEIC (see below). Source read at `main` (76b53778), where the cause is unchanged.

## What happens

`lightcraft-cli run --import <folder>` skips HEIC files in the folder, while the `library.import` command on the same folder takes them.

Folder `in/` holds two iPhone HEICs and one PNG.

```
$ lightcraft-cli run --import in library.selectAll
{"command":"library.selectAll","ms":0.4,"ok":true,"result":{"selected":1}}

$ lightcraft-cli run library.import 'paths=["in"]' library.selectAll
{"command":"library.import","ms":1.9,"ok":true,"result":{"duplicates":[],"failed":[],"imported":[1,2,3],"scanned":3,"sidecars":0}}
{"command":"library.selectAll","ms":0.0,"ok":true,"result":{"selected":3}}

$ lightcraft-cli run --import in/IMG_0682.heic --import in/map.png library.selectAll
{"command":"library.selectAll","ms":0.0,"ok":true,"result":{"selected":2}}
```

So the flag imports a HEIC when it is named explicitly, and the command imports HEICs from a folder, but the flag's folder walk leaves them out with no message. The help text says `--import PATH  headless, import a file or folder first (repeatable)`.

## Cause

Two extension lists have drifted apart.

- `crates/engine/src/import.rs:36` `EXTENSIONS` is what `library.import` uses through `is_supported()` (line 370). It includes `heic`, `heif`, `avif` and `nrw`.
- `crates/mcp/src/headless.rs:14` `PHOTO_EXTENSIONS` is what `expand_paths()` (line 179) uses when `--import` is given a directory. It lacks `heic`, `heif` and `nrw` (it has `avif`).

Diffing the two sets: engine only = `heic`, `heif`, `nrw`; CLI only = nothing. Everything else matches, so the CLI list looks like a copy that missed the later additions.

## Expected

`--import <folder>` and `library.import paths=[folder]` pick up the same files. The simplest fix is for `expand_paths` to call `lightcraft_engine::import::is_supported` (or use `EXTENSIONS`) instead of keeping its…

title: Auto Import: option to include subfolders of the watched folder
author: bitshiftza
body:
**Auto Import only watches the top level of its folder.** Files that land in a subfolder of the watched folder are never imported.

`list_auto_import_folder` (`crates/engine/src/cmd/library.rs`) lists the folder's direct entries and keeps only files, so anything inside a subfolder is skipped. Regular import is recursive, and Local browsing has a subfolders option, but Auto Import has neither.

**Why it matters:** many sources write into dated or per-device subfolders rather than one flat folder, for example tethering and capture tools, phone or camera sync apps (`DCIM/100CANON`, `2026/10/11/`), and cloud-drive camera uploads. Pointing Auto Import at the parent folder does nothing for them today.

**Proposal:** an **Include subfolders** option in Settings ▸ Import ▸ Auto Import, off by default so current behaviour doesn't change.
- When on, the watched folder is listed recursively, skipping hidden folders and the library's own folder, with a depth limit and a cap on entries so a huge or looping tree can't stall the scan.
- Symlinked folders aren't followed, to avoid loops.
- `library.autoImport` gains a `subfolders` setting, and `library.autoImportScan` reports it.
- How files are filed after import (move/copy, the destination layout) is unchanged.

title: Library folders: photo paths relative to a root, and Update Folder Location (a moved disk or folder is one change)
author: mattsivak
body:
## Problem (today, on one machine)

Every library photo stores an absolute path (`Source::File { path }`). When a disk or folder turns up somewhere else, every photo under it goes missing:

- a USB disk or NAS comes back at a new drive letter or mount point (`D:` → `E:`, `/Volumes/tokyo` → `/Volumes/tokyo 1`, `/media/me/usb` → `/run/media/me/usb`): Find Missing has to find every photo again, by name, size and content hash;
- the same disk written two ways shows as two disks (`/Volumes/tokyo` and `/Volumes/TOKYO`, LRC-LIB-LIBFOLDERS *Limits*);
- a folder moved outside LightCraft loses its colour label: Find Missing relinks photos but not folder records (same *Limits*);
- #1112: Synchronize Folder on a missing folder has no way to say where it went.

Lightroom Classic's answer is **Update Folder Location / Find Missing Folder** on a folder row: one change and everything under it follows. This issue proposes the same thing for LightCraft.

It's useful today, on a single machine, without any sync. It's also the per-device path mapping that multi-machine libraries (#294, #880) will need later, but nothing here depends on that plan or builds towards a sync format (no device ids, no clocks). It isn't a #641-style step that has no use yet.

## Design

**Roots.** The catalog keeps a table of roots, `Root { id, path, volume_name? }`. A photo's location becomes `(root, relative path)`. A root's `path` is where it is *on this machine*; `volume_name` (the mount or volume label as seen at import) is only kept for a later "this disk is back at E:\" prompt.

- On import, a photo goes under the deepest existing root that contains it; otherwise a new root is made at its disk (`folders::volume_of`: `D:`, `//server/share`, `/Volumes/tokyo`, `/media/me/usb` …). On the startup disk the root is `/` (or `C:`), until someone moves a folder there (below).
- The web build keeps one root for its OPFS storage. Local browse records (not library photos) stay on absolute paths.

title: [To discuss] DAM accessible across multiple machines
author: cajax
body:
Currently LC mimics the LR classic behavior, where the catalog belongs to a single computer where the app is running. The maximum what we can do is to export and then import this catalog on the other machine. But there are plenty of examples where DAM is available to multiple computers over cloud or local network. This can be useful for example to edit photos on the go or share work between team members.
I do not think it is a priority for anyone, so there is a plenty of time to discuss and pick the best solution.

One simplest idea, that doesn't even require any changes in LC itself - a standalone server that communicate to LC instances via MCP to fetch and send edits between them. A simple centralized storage that only update imports, deletions and edits. It would surely miss any locks and conflict resolution.
Later next week I will make a PoC for this variant as it is the cheapest, but I'm sure someone will suggest better ideas.

title: Per-command work on the UI thread: presets.json re-serialization dominates (fixed by #1056), the journal fsync remains; proposal: engine off the UI thread
author: THEtheChad
body:
## Summary

Every command (UI, control channel, MCP `--connect`) runs on the UI thread inside the frame: the egui app owns `Session` as `&mut` and `drain_control` executes queued requests from `logic()` (`crates/ui-egui/src/lib.rs:789-791`, called at `:993`). So whatever a command costs beyond its own work is frame time. I measured that overhead with a small benchmark (link below) on origin/main `76b53778`.

The results:

1. **Re-serializing `presets.json` after every command is the dominant overhead, and it scales with the user's preset count.** About 4-5 ms per command with 100 user presets, 20-25 ms with 500. That applies to every slider tick too. Open PR #1056 fixes this with a generation-stamped preset list. I measured its engine part with the same benchmark: the cost drops to about 1 µs per slider tick and 30-40 µs per committed command at any preset count.
2. **After that, the only per-command cost that matters is the journal `fsync`:** 2-4 ms per committed command on this machine. Commits from #37 measured 4-6 ms, and 7-15 ms under heavy load. Changing that changes the crash guarantee, so it is a maintainer decision (see the proposal below).
3. The other per-command work I checked costs too little to measure: the journal params clone, undo `Vec::remove(0)`, the history clone in `PushHistory`, the DevelopSettings clones and the `find_command` scan. I prototyped the cheap fixes (a HashMap command index, dropping one `Op` clone per commit and one DevelopSettings clone per `develop.set`). They made no difference I could tell from noise, so I'm not proposing them as a PR.

This issue records the measurements and puts one architecture option in front of the maintainers. That option is an engine that owns its state on its own thread. It relates to #718.

## Evidence

Per-command path on origin/main `76b53778`:

| Work | Where | Cost found |
|---|---|---|
| `persist()` after every top-level command | `crates/engine/src/lib.rs:463` | see below |
| `presets_json`: `se…

title: Performance: library queries scan lists per photo at 100k photos (stacks, albums, sort keys, rule matching)
author: THEtheChad
body:
## Summary

At 100k photos several library questions are answered by scanning a list once per photo, so their cost grows with photos × list length rather than with photos. The worst are a smart album with an "In a Stack" rule (2.7 s to count at 100k photos and 10k stacks), an album used as a filter or tested by a rule (0.6–0.8 s for a 20k-photo album), a manual album shown in its own order (2.0 s for 20k photos), and the File Name sort (lower-cases both names on every comparison). Most of these sit behind the sidebar's smart-album counts and the grid's query, so they run again after every catalog change.

This is separate from #1011 (the Keywords section; PR #1114 fixes the tree and draws only the rows in view) and from #1057 (develop edits invalidating every cache). Those two make the caches rebuild less often; this issue makes each rebuild cheaper.

## Evidence (main @ 76b53778)

Measured with a new ignored test, `cargo test --release -p lightcraft-catalog --lib scale_100k -- --ignored --nocapture`: 100,000 photos, 10,000 two-photo stacks, a 20,000-photo album, 500 keywords, best of five runs, release build on a shared 16-thread Linux box (WSL2) with other builds running, so treat the numbers as rough.

| Question at 100k photos | main |
|---|---|
| smart album count, "In a Stack" | 2,740 ms |
| query filtered to a 20k-photo album | 759 ms |
| smart album count, "Album is <20k album>" | 622 ms |
| query, File Name sort | 430 ms |
| query, `only` 5k ids | 145 ms |
| one batch adding 100k photos and 10k stacks | 1,671 ms |
| engine: a 20k-photo album shown in album order (`scale_100k_library_queries`) | 1,985 ms |
| `stack_of` × 1000 | 29 ms |

Where the time goes:

1. **`stack_of` is a scan of every stack** (`crates/catalog/src/stacks.rs:22-24`). The "stacked" rule calls it per photo (`crates/catalog/src/rules.rs:795`), so a smart album with that rule is O(photos × stacks). `validate_stack` also scans every stack on each `AddStack`/`SetStack` (`stacks.rs:43`), so b…

title: macOS: LightCraft-generated panorama DNG cannot be opened directly in LightCraft
author: doubledown00
body:
Bug report
Environment
- macOS 15.7.4
- Apple Silicon Mac
- LightCraft 0.5.0 when first observed
- Source files: Canon EOS 6D Mark II .CR2
- Panorama created with lightcraft-cli
Problem
A DNG created by LightCraft’s own panorama merge cannot be opened directly in the LightCraft GUI.
The panorama itself is created successfully with:
lightcraft-cli merge panorama --no-auto-settings *.CR2

The resulting file is a valid *-Pano.dng, and once it is available inside LightCraft it can be developed normally.
However, attempting to open the generated .dng directly in LightCraft produces an error stating:
cannot open files in Adobe raw image format

This is unexpected because the DNG was generated by LightCraft itself and LightCraft otherwise supports DNG/raw development.
Steps to reproduce
1. Start with two or more Canon CR2 files.
2. Create a panorama:
lightcraft-cli merge panorama --no-auto-settings IMG_1005.CR2 IMG_1006.CR2 IMG_1007.CR2

3. LightCraft creates:
IMG_1005-Pano.dng

4. Attempt to open that DNG directly with LightCraft from Finder/Open With.
5. LightCraft reports that it cannot open files in Adobe raw image format.
Expected behavior
A DNG generated by LightCraft should open directly in LightCraft the same way as other supported image/raw files.
Actual behavior
Direct opening is rejected with the Adobe RAW/DNG error.
Additional information
The generated panorama DNG itself appears valid and is usable once loaded into LightCraft, so this may be an application document-opening/file-type registration path rather than a DNG decoder failure.
Separately, panorama-generated DNGs observed during testing did not contain an AsShotNeutral or AsShotWhiteXY tag, causing a strong green cast until Auto White Balance was applied. That may be a separate issue, but I mention it in case the generated-DNG path is shared.
Status
Originally reproduced on LightCraft 0.5.0. Behavior still exists in 0.6.0.

title: Filmstrip shows the wrong place after switching to another album or source while the same photo stays active
author: PiMinusMax
body:
Switching between albums (or All Photographs, a folder, …) while the active photo is in both keeps the filmstrip at its old scroll offset. The photo sits at another place in the new source, so the strip shows other photos, and the active one is often off screen.

**Steps**
1. In All Photographs, select a photo far along the filmstrip.
2. Show an album that also holds this photo at another position.

**Expected:** the filmstrip (and the grid) scroll to the active photo.
**Actual:** they keep the old offset.

**Cause:** `grid::follow_active` only scrolls when the active photo *changes*; here it stays the same, only its index in the strip changes. The filmstrip's scroll area is shared by all sources, so the old offset carries over.

title: Masks are re-evaluated on every render: an Exposure drag with three masks costs 180-330 ms per loupe tick
author: THEtheChad
body:
## Summary

Every render evaluates every visible mask from scratch, on the CPU and on the GPU. The stage cache (`StageCache`, mirrored on the device by `GpuStages`) keeps the resampled image, the white-balanced/denoised image and the spatial planes, but not the mask alphas. So a global Exposure drag, or a drag of a mask's own Exposure / Clarity slider, re-rasterizes every brush, re-runs the range masks and heuristics, and re-runs Refine Edges' full-resolution guided filter, although none of those alphas changed.

On a 24 MP photo with three ordinary masks (a radial gradient, a three-stroke brush and either a linear gradient with Refine Edges 60 or a Subject mask), an Exposure drag tick on the CPU costs **176–332 ms at loupe size and 60–94 ms as a draft**. The same drag without masks costs about 27 ms (loupe). The budgets in `CLAUDE.md` are ≤ 60 ms (loupe) and ≤ 16 ms (draft).

Two smaller findings in the same code:

- Both caches under-report their memory. `StageCache::bytes` and `GpuStages::bytes` leave out the blurred chromaticity plane (12 B/px, built whenever a mask has Noise or Moiré). Those numbers feed `trim_stages` against the memory budget.
- The loops that combine, invert, refine and scale mask components run serially over w × h. The rest of the pipeline runs row-parallel (`for_rows`).

## Evidence (origin/main 76b53778)

- `crates/pipeline/src/local.rs:539`: `prepare` calls `masks::evaluate(&s.masks, …)` unconditionally on every render.
- `crates/pipeline/src/lib.rs:243` (`StageCache`), `:341` (`CacheEntry`: `src`, `geo`, `sampled`, `lin`, `planes`) and the keys built in `plan()` at `:426` (`geo`) and `:441` (`lin_key`). There is no slot for alphas.
- `crates/gpu/src/render.rs:662`: `masks(&mut cx, &lin, &prep, &plan, &mut host)` runs on every GPU render. Shapes without a kernel (Sky, Subject, Background, People, Object heuristics) read `lin` and `log_l` back from the device, evaluate on the CPU and upload, on every tick (`render.rs:~1050`).

title: Zoom windows: the 768 px margin cap leaves Dehaze up to 49 LSB off at 8:1 (14 LSB at 4:1)
author: THEtheChad
body:
## Summary

A zoom window (#323) renders the visible part of the zoomed frame plus a margin of context, so that the wide stages (Dehaze's dark channel and airlight, the Clarity and Highlights / Shadows base planes) see what lies around the visible edge. `margin_for` asks for 4.5 % of the zoomed frame's long edge but caps it at 768 px (`crates/ui-egui/src/region.rs:14` `MAX_MARGIN`, `:45-48`). Those stages' sigmas scale with the long edge (up to 2 % of it, per the comment), so the cap starts to bind at about 3:1 on a 24 MP photo. From 4:1 on, the visible pixels come out measurably different from the same pixels of a whole-frame render (the export): **up to 14 LSB at 4:1 and 49 LSB at 8:1 with Dehaze 100**, and up to 76 LSB at 11:1 with strong Dehaze + Clarity + Shadows / Highlights. Because the error depends on where the window sits, the same pixels can also render differently after a pan picks a new window (snapped to 256 px).

## Evidence

- `margin_for(full_long) = ceil256(min(0.045 · full_long, 768))`. For a 6000 px (24 MP) photo the zoomed long edge is 18,000 px at 3:1, 24,000 at 4:1, 48,000 at 8:1 and 66,000 at 11:1, so the margin is 0.043, 0.032, 0.016 and 0.0116 of the long edge. For a 60 MP photo (9504 px) at 1:1 the cap doesn't bind: 427 rounds up to 512 px, or 0.054.
- Measured with the pipeline's own window renders (`RenderRequest::window`, the path the loupe uses, including the whole-frame airlight proxy): a 400×300 visible region in the middle of a 2400×1600 frame (procedural `blocks()` source), rendered once as part of the whole frame and once as a window with a margin of the given fraction of the long edge. The stages scale with the long edge (resolution independence), so the fractions carry over to the zoomed sizes above. Max and mean |Δ| over the visible region, 8-bit RGB:

```
dehaze 60                      margin 0.000 of long (   0 px): max  50 LSB, mean 0.837 LSB
dehaze 60                      margin 0.012 of long (  28 px): max  37 LSB, mean 0.…

body:
**Version:** LightCraft 0.6.0 (portable, `lightcraft-0.6.0-windows-x64-portable`)
**Platform:** Windows 11 x86_64
**Component:** `apps/lightcraft-cli/src/main.rs` (argument parsing), verified against tag `v0.6.0`

> **Severity: low.** This is a diagnostics/ergonomics problem, not a broken feature —
> every form that is documented to work does work, and no invocation silently
> produces a wrong *result*. Details of why the parser behaves this way are at the
> bottom; I'm mainly suggesting two small improvements.

## What happens

`--connect` takes an optional address. A value is only consumed when it contains a
colon (tag `v0.6.0`, `apps/lightcraft-cli/src/main.rs:509`, in `run_step`):

```rust
"--connect" => match args.get(i + 1).filter(|a| a.contains(':') && !a.contains('=')) {
    Some(a) => { i += 1; connect = Some(a.clone()); }
    None => connect = Some(DEFAULT_ADDR.to_string()),
},
```

`lightcraft-cli --help` advertises:

```
--connect [ADDR]  drive the running app (`lightcraft --control 7980`; default 127.0.0.1:7980)
```

so `lightcraft-cli run --connect 7980 ui.inspect` is a natural thing to type after
starting the app with `--control 7980`. The port is not consumed, the CLI uses the
default address instead, and `7980` is then parsed as a command id.

## Steps to reproduce

```powershell
# with a live app:  .\lightcraft.exe --control 7980
.\lightcraft-cli.exe run --connect 7980 ui.inspect
```

## Actual

With the app running on the default address (`127.0.0.1:7980`), so the fallback
address happens to be correct:

```json
{"command":"7980","error":"unknown command `7980`","ok":false}
lightcraft-cli: 1 command(s) failed
```

With no app running, the connection error comes first and hides the parsing
behaviour — note that the address in the message is the *default*, and `7980` was
never used as the address:

```
lightcraft-cli: LightCraft is not reachable at 127.0.0.1:7980 (connection timed out); start it with `lightcraft --control 7980`
```

title: Docs: no written contribution workflow, and AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md have drifted
author: clydecbrown
body:
## Summary

A new contributor (human, or an agent working for one) who follows the README's "read AGENTS.md first" finds the contribution workflow unwritten and two instruction files that disagree. Neither affects the app.

1. **No contribution workflow is written down.** There is no `CONTRIBUTING.md`, PR template or issue template (`.github/` holds only `workflows/`; issue templates are #648). As I understand it from Discord, the convention is to comment on an issue to claim it, then open a PR with `Fixes #N` in the description, but that appears nowhere in the repo. Without it, duplicate work happens: #1119 and #1175 both fix #1080.
2. **`AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` have drifted.** #161 fixed both files on the basis that they stay identical; they no longer are:
   - only `CLAUDE.md` has the activity-stack rule (`cad9782c`), the `TextField` rule (`aec847a2`) and the other-scripts font fallback (`d803d905`);
   - only `AGENTS.md` has the "Contributor credits (About window)" section (#252).

   So humans (sent to `AGENTS.md` by the README) miss two required rules, and Claude agents (which read `CLAUDE.md`) miss the rule to ask their human about credits.

## Suggested fix

- Add a short `CONTRIBUTING.md`: claim an issue by commenting, PR with `Fixes #N`, title prefixed with the task / checklist id, `cargo xtask ci` green, the checklist / gaps / ROADMAP updates expected in the same commit, and where to ask (Discord). Link it from the README's Contributing section.
- Make `AGENTS.md` the single source and `CLAUDE.md` a pointer to it (`@AGENTS.md`), with the four diverging sections merged in, so the two can't drift again.

## Evidence

- `main` at `76b53778`; `diff CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md` shows the four sections above.
- Related: #161 (closed), #648 (issue templates, open); the craftrules / `plan/` part is #1183.

I'd like to take this one and will open a PR with `Fixes` for it.

title: Feature request: Locate missing files for a folder / folder tree
author: csidirop
body:
LightCraft currently allows locating an individual missing photo via: *Right click photo → Locate Missing File*

When an entire folder or folder tree has been moved or after an LR library import however, every missing photo has to be handled individually from the UI. Fixing the location for one image does not recursevly find other missing near pictures (like its done in LR). This is especially cumbersome after moving a photo archive to another disk, NAS path, mount point, or reorganized directory.

## Simplest solution

Add a similar action to the folder context menu, for example: *Right click folder → Locate Missing Files*

The user would select the folder's new location, and LightCraft would attempt to relink all missing files belonging to that folder and its subfolders. Ideally, the existing folder structure should be preserved. For example:

```text
Old:
D:\Photos\2024\Trip\IMG_001.jpg
D:\Photos\2024\Trip\Day2\IMG_002.jpg

New:
E:\Archive\Photos\2024\Trip\IMG_001.jpg
E:\Archive\Photos\2024\Trip\Day2\IMG_002.jpg
```

Selecting `E:\Archive\Photos\2024\Trip` for the missing `Trip` folder should relink both files, including files in subfolders.

## Existing functionality

The engine already appears to provide most of the required functionality through `library.findMissing`, including recursive scanning and bulk relinking. Also there is an UI element found in _File → Locate Missing Files _ which does exactly that. Therefore, this may mainly require exposing the existing functionality through the folder/sidebar UI.

## Use cases

- Moving a photo library to another disk
- Changing NAS/server paths
- Restoring a library from backup
- Reorganizing folders outside LightCraft
- Importing/migrating catalogs where the original paths no longer exist

This would make recovery of moved folder trees significantly easier than locating each missing photo individually.

title: Arch Linux / AUR builds OOM on 16 GB systems during release linking (candle/wgpu + LTO)
author: rajchauhan28
body:
### Description

When building `lightcraft` on Arch Linux via the AUR package (`lightcraft-0.6.0-1`) or when building release binaries from source on machines with 16 GB RAM and high CPU thread counts (e.g. 16–20 threads), the build consistently fails due to Out-Of-Memory kills (`systemd-oomd` / kernel OOM-killer) during the final linking step.

### Environment
- **OS**: Arch Linux / CachyOS (Linux 7.2.x)
- **CPU**: Intel Core i5-13500HX (20 threads)
- **RAM**: 16 GB RAM + 16 GB Swap/Zram
- **AUR Package**: `lightcraft 0.6.0-1` (Maintainer: Caleb Maclennan)

### Cause of OOM
During `cargo build --release`, Cargo builds both `lightcraft` and `lightcraft-cli` concurrently. Because the workspace includes heavy dependencies (`candle-core`, `wgpu`, `egui`, `liblightcraft_web.so`), linking both binaries simultaneously requires substantial memory.

In the AUR package, the build environment also specifies:
```bash
export CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=2
export CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=false
export CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=thin
export CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=1
```
The combination of `DEBUG=2` (generating massive DWARF symbols) and `CODEGEN_UNITS=1` + `LTO=thin` causes rustc's codegen unit (`lto cgu.0.rcgu.`) to consume over 6–7 GB RSS per process. When both binaries link in parallel on a high-thread system, peak memory usage exceeds 10 GB RSS and 9 GB swap, triggering `systemd-oomd` and terminating the terminal session:

```text
kernel: lto cgu.0.rcgu.: page allocation failure: order:0, mode:0xc0de0
systemd-oomd[1029]: Marked ... for killing due to memory used (16.4 GB) / total (16.4 GB) and swap used (14.8 GB) / total (16.4 GB) being more than 90.00%
systemd[1289]: app-ghostty-...scope: systemd-oomd killed 84 process(es) in this unit.
systemd[1289]: app-ghostty-...scope: Failed with result 'oom-kill'.
```

### Resolution
The build succeeds reliably on 16 GB systems by:
1. Limiting concurrent cargo jobs (e.g. `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=1` or `2`) so both large binaries a…

title: Feature Request – Focus Stacking and Astrophotography Stacking
author: SebUll
body:
Hi LightCraft team,

I'm currently evaluating LightCraft as a complete replacement for Adobe Lightroom and potentially other photography applications.
I'm using a Sony Alpha 1 and frequently work with macro photography, wildlife, landscapes, panoramas, and astrophotography.
I noticed that LightCraft already supports HDR, panorama stitching, and HDR panoramas, which is fantastic!

However, I couldn't find dedicated features for focus stacking or astrophotography stacking.

Would it be possible to add the following functionality?

Focus Stacking:

- Automatic alignment of images captured at different focus distances.
- Automatic detection and merging of the sharpest areas.
- Support for high-resolution RAW files.
- High-quality output as TIFF or DNG.
- Ideally, a simple workflow directly through Photo Merge → Focus Stack.

Astrophotography:

- Automatic star alignment across multiple exposures.
- Image stacking with noise reduction.
- Dark, flat, and bias frame calibration.
- Sigma-clipping or other rejection algorithms for satellites and unwanted artifacts.
- Support for wide-field astrophotography, Milky Way photography, and deep-sky imaging.
- High-resolution TIFF or DNG output.

Ideally, both features should be available directly through LightCraft's existing Photo Merge workflow, without requiring external software.

Are any of these features already planned?

Thanks for your continued work on LightCraft!

title: Fujifilm recipe inspector: show MakerNote film settings
author: MohammadTeimori
body:
## Summary

Fujifilm RAF and JPEG files already carry the in-camera film recipe in the MakerNote (film simulation, dynamic range, white-balance shift, grain, highlight/shadow, Color Chrome, and related steps). LightCraft parses the `FUJIFILM` MakerNote IFD, but those tags are not named or shown.

This proposes a **read-only** inspector. It does not change pixels, add a film-simulation color engine, or generate presets.

## Proposed v1

- Decode the public FujiFilm MakerNote tags from the embedded JPEG EXIF (RAF) and from a camera JPEG.
- Show a card in the Info panel when a Fujifilm note is present, with a Copy action for the plain-text lines.
- Expose the same data as a query command so CLI and MCP can read it.
- Name the same rows in All Metadata (`photo.allMetadata`).
- Unknown codes display as `Unknown (n)`. A custom recipe name such as C1 is not stored in the file, so it is not recovered.

Tags: film simulation `0x1401` (plus Acros / B&W filter from `0x1003`), dynamic range `0x1402` / `0x1400`, white balance `0x1002` and Kelvin `0x1005`, shift `0x100a`, grain `0x1047` / `0x104c`, highlight `0x1041`, shadow `0x1040`, Color Chrome `0x1048`, Color Chrome FX Blue `0x104e`, sharpness `0x1001`, noise reduction `0x100e` or `0x100b`, clarity `0x100f`.

## Out of scope

- Reproducing Classic Chrome / Eterna / Acros (that remains #380).
- A recipe library, recipe cards as files, or approximate LightCraft presets.
- Catalog search by film simulation.

## Tests

Synthetic MakerNotes only in the repository. Personal camera files stay local and are checked against ExifTool, not committed.

Is the Info-panel card the right place, or would you rather this land only inside All Metadata?

title: Explore calibration-first RAW colour, with optional camera-JPEG appearance matching
author: QuirkyTurtle94
body:
While investigating the Sony colour issues discussed in #763 and the narrower fix in #732, I reviewed darktable’s RAW development pipeline. I’d like to discuss whether LightCraft should move towards **camera calibration as the default colour foundation**, while retaining embedded-JPEG matching as an optional appearance mode or fallback.

This is a proposal for an experiment and architectural discussion, rather than a request to immediately replace the existing pipeline.

**Current behaviour**

LightCraft already supports embedded colour matrices, per-model profiles and matrices derived from measured spectral sensitivities. However, for RAWs without an embedded matrix, an accepted fit to the camera JPEG can take precedence over the model’s spectral matrices.

The JPEG is used to estimate a transformation; LightCraft still renders pixels from the RAW sensor data. The concern is therefore scene-dependent colour estimation, rather than JPEG pixel replacement.

The current approach has understandable advantages: broad camera coverage and a starting appearance closer to the camera’s rendering. But a photograph containing mostly foliage, grey tones or one saturated colour gives limited evidence about the camera’s response elsewhere in colour space. Holding out pixels from that same image tests the fit within that scene; it does not establish consistency across other scenes or lighting.

The reference JPEG also contains the camera’s tone mapping, picture style, highlight treatment and potentially local adjustments. Matching it is a different objective from establishing a stable sensor-to-working-space conversion.

[LightCraft’s current selection order](https://github.com/storytold/lightcraft/blob/76b5377868d912db69a777bda253a5b1b96b22bd/crates/engine/src/camera_preview.rs#L64)

**What prompted this proposal**

In the darktable source reviewed, supported RAWs normally use a camera-specific input matrix/profile, with white balance and chromatic adaptation handled explicitly. …

title: Transparent PNG areas turn black in rendered JPEGs and contact sheets
author: PrismaDiamond
body:
**What I ran** (lightcraft-cli 0.6.0, linux-aarch64):

```
lightcraft-cli render alpha.png -o out.jpg
lightcraft-cli run --import alpha.png library.selectAll export.contactSheet path=sheet.pdf columns=1 rows=1
```

`alpha.png` is 200×100 RGBA: the left half opaque red, the right half fully transparent (stored as RGB 0,0,0 with alpha 0, as most encoders write it). Script to make it:

```python
import struct, zlib
w, h = 200, 100
rows = [b"\x00" + b"".join(bytes([220, 40, 40, 255]) if x < w // 2 else bytes(4) for x in range(w)) for _ in range(h)]
c = lambda t, d: struct.pack(">I", len(d)) + t + d + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(t + d) & 0xffffffff)
open("alpha.png", "wb").write(b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + c(b"IHDR", struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", w, h, 8, 6, 0, 0, 0))
                             + c(b"IDAT", zlib.compress(b"".join(rows))) + c(b"IEND", b""))
```

**What happens:** the transparent half is black, both in `out.jpg` and on the contact sheet.

**Expected:** transparency flattened onto white, as Photoshop does when it saves a JPEG and as PhotoCraft's `photocraft-cli convert alpha.png out.jpg` does. Black backgrounds make logos, screenshots with rounded corners and cut-outs unusable.

**Likely cause** (reading `main` 76b53778): the decoders keep the alpha plane (`crates/codecs/src/other.rs` → `Decoded.alpha`), but the develop path starts from `lightcraft_codecs::to_working()` (`crates/codecs/src/lib.rs:247`), which converts `d.image` only and ignores `d.alpha`. Fully transparent pixels therefore keep whatever colour they store, usually black. Compositing onto white there (or at export, for formats without alpha) would fix both outputs.

---
Environment: lightcraft-cli 0.6.0, Linux aarch64 (Raspberry Pi 5, Debian 13), headless CLI.

title: Hidden and empty masks change Clarity through tone-base selection
author: AlexChambers
body:
On main `76b53778`, a hidden mask or a mask with no components can change visible
Clarity output. Its Highlights and Shadows values select a filtered tone base.
Clarity reads that base even when global Highlights and Shadows are zero.

## Reproduction

1. Generate a 600 by 400 linear RGB image. For pixel `(x, y)`, set
   `l = 0.003 + (((x * 17 + y * 23) % 103) / 102.0)^2` and RGB to
   `[1.1 * l, l, 0.8 * l]`.
2. Set global Clarity to 100. Leave global Highlights and Shadows at zero.
3. Add a hidden linear mask, starting at `(0.1, 0.2)` and ending at `(0.9, 0.8)`.
   Set its Highlights to -80 and Shadows to 80.
4. Render at 1200 by 800 with `window=None`. Compare with the same settings after
   removing that mask. Repeat with a visible mask whose component list is empty.

Both inactive mask cases produce the same differences on the CPU:

| Process | Changed pixels out of 960,000 | Maximum RGB code difference | Mean absolute RGB code difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| V1 | 599,946 | 19 | 1.650773 |
| V2 | 635,521 | 18 | 1.603042 |

Visible local Clarity 100 also reproduces it. Using the same linear mask for
Clarity changes 485,244 pixels in V1 and 500,092 in V2, with maxima of 19 and 18.
The independent round 2 review reproduced the global case on Metal as well.

## Cause and compatibility

`local::plane_sigmas` considers every mask when selecting the tone base. Mask
evaluation later excludes hidden and empty masks, but the finish stage still
uses the selected base to weight Clarity. CPU and GPU share this dependency.

An inactive mask should not affect visible pixels. However, changing this
selection changes existing V1 and V2 renders. The #1146 window-context fix keeps
main's behavior and includes the base's support whenever active Clarity reads
it. Resolve the unwanted dependency separately with an explicit compatibility
decision.

These are procedural measurements; no images or proprietary assets are needed. Found while working on the #1146 window-context fix.

title: Header plan describes an ARW6 strip from part of it: the import probe fails where the whole file decodes
author: mdlmarkham
body:
`sparse::header_plan` / `preview_plan` promise that once they say `Ready`, probing the partly loaded buffer gives
exactly what probing the whole file gives. That promise breaks for a Sony ARW6 (TIFF Compression 32766, RawDB's
`arw6/ILCE-7RM6_APSC_land_RAW-C-HD.ARW`, CC0, one of the two files `cargo xtask corpus --download` fetches):

```
crates/raw/tests/sparse_corpus.rs: arw6-sony-ilce7rm6-apsc-land-hq.arw: differs from the whole file
  left:  Err(Unsupported("ARW6 first-half row count outside 2..=7"))
  right: Ok(RawInfo { format: Arw, width: 6592, ... })
```

`tiff_plan` holes a compression-32766 strip behind its first 64 KiB, but the ARW6 header probe validates more than
a prefix there: per tile it walks the 13 stream header words, reads every stream's index table, and decodes the
residual stream's first half — which sits behind the earlier streams' data, megabytes into the strip. With those
bytes unloaded the probe reads zeros (and 0xFF), the residual's line count goes out of range, and the import probe
describes a file that actually opens as an error (the inverse direction too: a broken file probes as fine when its
corrupt bytes are holed).

The other corpus formats pass the same test for fills 0 and 0xFF; only the ARW6 pair (APS-C HQ, full-frame
Compressed — the four-tile case) fails, because their stream layout puts the residual's first half past the
prefix. Nothing in CI catches it: the corpus is git-ignored, and ARW6 shipped merged that same day (#961's module
is from #832's step 1). Fixed in #1223 (`Fixes`), with a synthetic no-corpus regression so it stays fixed when the
corpus is absent.

Cross-links: #1020 (the plan-preview loader; its PR description documents this failure as pre-existing) and #832
(the batched import this module serves — ARW6 originals currently probe 26-28% of the file with the JPEG-interchange
image unholed too, ~1-2% once #1223 lands).

title: Loupe: hand GPU renders to egui without a CPU readback (share the wgpu device)
author: mattsivak
body:
## Problem

When the GPU renders the loupe, every frame makes a round trip through the CPU before it reaches the screen:

1. `lightcraft_gpu` makes its own wgpu instance and device (`crates/gpu/src/ctx.rs`, around lines 286-313).
2. Each render is read back by `finish_and_read` (`ctx.rs`, around line 535). It copies into a staging buffer, calls `map_async` and waits with `poll(Wait)`. The result becomes an `Rgba8` buffer.
3. On the UI thread, `color_image()` (`crates/ui-egui/src/render.rs`, around line 93) converts it pixel by pixel. Then `tex.set()` / `ctx.load_texture` (`render.rs`, around lines 729-739) uploads it to egui. egui runs on eframe's own wgpu device, a different one (eframe 0.36; `apps/lightcraft/src/window_gpu.rs` picks Wgpu, with Glow as the fallback).

At 1:1 on a large raw this costs more than the render does. Measured on PR #1009 ([benchmark comment](https://github.com/storytold/lightcraft/pull/1009#issuecomment-6119762599)) on an Apple M3 Max, with a 61 MP Sony raw at 1:1 in a 2800x1700 Retina viewport:

- The 1:1 window is 3840x2816, about 43 MB of RGBA per tick.
- The whole-image GPU jobs take 7-9 ms (median).
- Complete texture updates take 18.3-30 ms (median). **0 of 234 met the 16 ms slider budget.**

Most of the difference is the readback, the conversion and the upload.

## Proposal

When the window renders with wgpu, give `lightcraft_gpu` eframe's device and queue (from `egui_wgpu::RenderState`) instead of creating its own, so both use the same adapter. Render the loupe into a wgpu texture that stays on the GPU, and pass it to egui with `egui_wgpu::Renderer::register_native_texture` (or `update_egui_texture_from_wgpu_texture` when the size has not changed). That removes the readback, the per-pixel conversion and the upload.

## Considerations

- **Device sharing:** only possible when the window uses wgpu. The GPU context then has to be built from eframe's `RenderState`, after the window exists (related: #410). The adapter, features and lim…

title: Optional RAW+JPEG paired culling
author: MohammadTeimori
body:

Detect by directory and stem, plus capture time and camera when both sides have them. Do not pair subfolder exports, two raws, or disagreeing metadata. Store the link. Splitting or turning the feature off leaves both photos, files, and sidecars. Optionally write ratings and pick/reject to both in one undo step; colour labels are a separate preference. Delete never follows the partner. Optionally show one grid cell, with the JPEG on screen and the raw still available for editing.

Out of scope: one catalog photo, automatic JPEG skip, HEIC, and raw-pipeline changes.

title: HEIC imports carry no EXIF (no capture date)
author: radialmonster
body:
HEIC/HEIF photos import and decode since 0.6.0, but they carry no metadata: `photo.allMetadata` shows `exif: []`, so there are no capture dates, camera or lens fields, and date sorting and filtering don't work for them. Reported in #693 on a library of ~35,750 iPhone HEICs.

**Cause (main 25ef65c8):** `lightcraft_meta::extract` calls `container::embedded` (`crates/meta/src/container.rs:30`), which knows RAF, CR3, JPEG, PNG, WebP and TIFF-based files. There is no branch for the ISO base media `ftyp` HEIF/HEIC/AVIF brands, so HEICs get an empty `Embedded`.

The data is already there: the HEIF decoder returns the EXIF block as a TIFF structure (`crates/heif/src/lib.rs:91-93`, passed on in `crates/codecs/src/heif.rs:90`), along with XMP. It just never reaches the metadata path.

**Fix:** add a HEIF branch to `container::embedded` that returns the `Exif` item (offset header stripped) and the XMP `mime` item, the way the CR3 branch does. Re-reading metadata on existing libraries would then fill in the dates.

title: Lightroom catalog import: per-table size caps drop all edits from large catalogs (stream rows instead)
author: bitshiftza
body:
**Lightroom catalog import drops every edit, with only a warning, when the develop settings table is over 256 MiB.**

The importer's SQLite reader (`crates/engine/src/lightroom_sqlite.rs`) decodes a whole table into memory before the importer uses it, so it caps each table at 256 MiB of record payload (`MAX_TABLE_PAYLOAD`) and one million rows (`MAX_ROWS`). #842 makes the reader page through the file instead of loading it whole, which fixes the 1 GiB file limit (#798), but it keeps these per-table caps, so large catalogs still hit them.

Two problems:

1. **Large tables are capped regardless of how much the importer actually needs.** A long-used catalog's `Adobe_imageDevelopSettings`, `Adobe_libraryImageDevelopHistoryStep` and `Adobe_AdditionalMetadata` easily pass 256 MiB. Measured on a real 1.08 GiB Lightroom Classic 13.5 catalog (60,485 photos): develop history 501 MiB on disk, develop settings 278 MiB. Catalogs mentioned in #798 are 1.5 GB and 13 GB.
2. **Develop settings are read as an optional table.** An optional table over a cap is skipped with a warning (`skipping optional Lightroom table …`). For `Adobe_imageDevelopSettings` that means **every photo arrives without its Lightroom edits**, and the import otherwise looks successful. Someone migrating a large catalog can easily miss the warning.

**Proposal**
- Stream table rows to the importer instead of collecting whole tables, so memory depends on what the importer keeps (the columns it maps), not on the table's size. The per-table payload and row caps can then go or rise to match the file cap; per-value bounds (`MAX_PAYLOAD`, XMP limits) stay.
- Treat the develop settings table as required for edits: if it can't be read, the import fails with a clear error, or (at minimum) reports prominently that edits were not imported and for how many photos, never a quiet warning.
- Keep history and snapshots optional (they go to the recovery archive, not native history), but bounded by streaming rather than skipped wh…

title: Dehaze is far too strong: haze estimate treats ordinary tones as haze (−0.8 EV at +50, black halos from +10)
author: mattsivak
body:
Dehaze is far too strong and isn't usable at normal values: even +20–30 darkens the whole photo, crushes shadows to black and draws dark halos around bright areas. The cause is how haze is estimated, not just the slider gain.

## Where
- `crates/pipeline/src/finish.rs` (the `// --- dehaze (scene linear)` block)
- `crates/pipeline/src/local.rs`: the haze plane is `gaussian(dark_of(..))` with sigma = 2 % of the long edge; airlight = 99.5th percentile of that plane.

This code hasn't changed since M0.4 and was tuned by eye.

## Why it's too strong
1. **Ordinary tones count as haze.** The dark-channel prior relies on a *minimum over a patch*, which is about 0 in haze-free areas. We use a *Gaussian blur* of the per-pixel `min(r,g,b)`. For neutral or muted pixels that's roughly the pixel's own brightness, so `t = 1 − 0.95·s·d` subtracts the brightness itself. At +100 every tone below the airlight is scaled by about 0.05 (−4.3 EV).
2. **Halos.** The wide blur carries bright sky into the foreground's haze estimate, so `v − A·(1 − t)` goes negative and the `.max(0)` clips it. A shadow pixel (0.05) beside bright sky (blurred d = 0.7, A = 0.8) clips to pure black at **+10**.
3. **No gentle range.** +100 maps to the prior's maximum (ω = 0.95, t floor 0.12) and the slider scales linearly. Negative dehaze blends up to 70 % toward 0.9·A, which washes the photo out.

## Numbers
Simulated: brightness change of a neutral tone sitting in a neighbourhood of the same tone (A = 0.8):

| tone | +10 | +25 | +50 | +75 | +100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.05 | −0.14 EV | −0.37 | −0.89 | −1.73 | −4.23 |
| 0.18 | −0.11 | −0.31 | −0.77 | −1.55 | −3.97 |
| 0.40 | −0.07 | −0.21 | −0.54 | −1.16 | −3.39 |

Measured: `lightcraft-cli render docs/images/grid-pd.jpg --size 900 --set effects.dehaze=N` (8-bit luma):

| dehaze | mean | median | p90 | pixels < 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 40.9 | 36 | 85 | 6.3 % |
| +25 | 33.6 | 26 | 77 | 14.4 % |
| +50 | 26.7 | 11 | 67 | 26.8 % |
| +100 | 15.0 | 0 | 3…

title: Deleting a photo doesn't ask for confirmation (off by default; right-click Delete Photo never asks)
author: mattsivak
body:
Deleting a photo happens with no question asked. Pressing Delete, choosing Photo ▸ Delete Photo, or right-clicking a photo and choosing **Delete Photo** moves it to Recently Deleted at once. Lightroom Classic always asks first.

## Why
- **Settings ▸ General ▸ "Confirm before moving photos to Recently Deleted"** (`AppSettings::confirm_delete`) exists, but it **defaults to off** (`crates/ui-egui/src/state.rs`, `confirm_delete: false`). Unless you know to turn it on, every delete happens silently.
- **The grid's right-click "Delete Photo" ignores the setting entirely** (`crates/ui-egui/src/panels/grid.rs`, it runs `photo.delete` directly). The keyboard (`shortcuts.rs`) and the menu bar (`menubar.rs`) both go through `menus::confirm_delete`, so even with the setting on, the context menu deletes without asking.

## Expected
- Delete asks before photos move to Recently Deleted, by default, from every entry point (key, menu bar, context menu).
- The setting stays, so people who don't want the question can turn it off.

Related: #565 (Remove from Catalog vs Delete from Disk), #298.

title: Nikon D7100 NEFs develop larger than Lightroom's frame, so Lightroom crops land up to 6 px off (18 px in full frame)
author: AlexChambers
body:
LightCraft develops Nikon D7100 NEFs a little larger than Lightroom does. The extra pixels sit evenly around Lightroom's frame, so the picture itself lines up, but a full-frame render has a few more pixels at each edge. A crop read from Lightroom (XMP sidecar or catalog) is normalised to Lightroom's frame and applied to LightCraft's larger one, so its edges move by up to 6 px at full size on 1.3x crop files and up to 18 px on full-frame files.

## Reproduction

The files are public, from [zjqc/photographing-art](https://github.com/zjqc/photographing-art) (MIT): Nikon D7100 raws in `lr raw备份/` with Lightroom Classic 12.0 exports elsewhere in the repo. Each export embeds the `crs:` settings it was made with.

| File | Raw crop (ExifTool `CropHiSpeed`) | LightCraft render, no edits | Lightroom export at full size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DSC_2763.NEF`, export `慕田峪/修_DSC_2763.jpg` (no crop, Upright Off) | 1.3x crop: 6036x4020 cropped to 4812x3212 | 4812 × 3212 | 4800 × 3200 |
| `DSC_1316.NEF`, export `人物、动物/芸芸众生-山上的建筑工.jpg` (no crop, shown in portrait) | Off: 6036x4020 | 4020 × 6036 | 4000 × 6000 |

`lightcraft-cli render DSC_2763.NEF -o out.png` on main 76b5377 writes 4812 × 3212.

## Where the extra pixels are

I matched each LightCraft render to Lightroom's export with SIFT features, fitted a homography with RANSAC and refined it by least squares on the inliers. Lightroom's frame is LightCraft's with the extra pixels shared equally between opposite sides:

- **1.3x crop files:** 6 px trimmed on every side. DSC_2763, Upright Off, matches with that inset to 0.46 px mean and 0.79 px max at full size. DSC_1486, shown in portrait and cropped, matches to 0.48 / 0.86 px.
- **Full-frame file:** 18 px trimmed at the left and right of the stored image, 10 px at the top and bottom. DSC_1316 matches to 0.1 px mean once its Upright is accounted for.

## Effect on crops

Lightroom's crop edges are fractions of its 4800 × 3200 frame. LightCraft applies the same fractions to 4812 × 32…

title: New Album always adds the selected photos: add Lightroom's "Include selected photos" option
author: MarkusFriedel
body:
**What happens now**
Creating an album (File ▸ New Album…, Albums ▸ + ▸ Create Album…, or right-click ▸ Add to Album ▸ New Album…) always puts the selected photos into it. To create an empty album you first have to deselect everything, which isn't possible in Detail view (the photo shown counts as selected), or remove the photos again afterwards.

**What Lightroom does**
Lightroom Classic's Create Collection dialog has an **Include selected photos** checkbox. It only appears when photos are selected.

**Proposal**
- An "Include selected photos" checkbox in the New Album dialog, ticked by default so today's behaviour stays the default.
- Like Lightroom, it only appears when something is selected, and never for folders.
- `dialog.newAlbum` takes an optional `includeSelected` so agents and the CLI can preset it.

The engine already supports this (`album.create {addSelected}`), so it's a small UI change. I have a PR ready.

title: Assisted Culling blocks the UI thread on large selections and recomputes all scores on re-run
author: Archolas
body:
## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Version | LightCraft 0.6.0 (standalone `.msi`) |
| OS | Windows [10/11, build] |
| Hardware | [CPU / GPU / RAM] |
| Files | ~2,120 Panasonic `.RW2` from one event, local folder (OneDrive-synced, files kept on device) |

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open a folder of ~2,000 raws.
2. With no selection, choose **Photo ▸ Assisted Culling…** and confirm.
3. When it finishes, run **Assisted Culling…** again on the same photos.

## Actual behaviour

- The window freezes immediately and Windows shows **"LightCraft is not responding"**, offering to close it.
- It completes after [~X minutes] with correct results, but there's no progress indicator or cancel. Choosing "Close the program" at the Windows prompt would lose the whole run.
- The second run repeats the **full analysis from scratch**, with the same freeze, even though every photo already has a stored `Analysis` (focus, clipping, group).

## Expected behaviour

- The analysis runs on a background worker with progress and ✕ cancel in the activity stack, like import, **Synchronize Folder** and the denoise queue, so the window stays responsive.
- A re-run reuses stored measurements for unchanged files and only re-groups and applies the new flags, so changing **Reject below** or **Pick best** is instant. An explicit "Re-analyse" option could force a fresh pass.

## Likely cause

`photo.analyze` (`crates/engine/src/cmd/cull.rs`, `analyze`) calls `s.source_now(id, SourceLevel::Thumb)` followed by `cull::sharpness`, `cull::clipped` and `cull::signature` for every photo in a synchronous loop, invoked from the dialog via `app.run("photo.analyze", …)` (`crates/ui-egui/src/panels/dialogs.rs`, `Dialog::Cull`).

Nothing is cached between runs. `library.findSimilar` already caches signatures by content key in `s.signatures`, and that cache plus the photo's stored `Analysis` could be reused here.

title: Import into an album from its context menu
author: MarkusFriedel
body:
**What happens now**
An album's context menu has no way to import into it. You always go through File ▸ Import…, then pick the album in the review's Album dropdown, which lists every album in one flat list, without their folders. With many albums (e.g. one per event, dozens per season inside folders), finding the right one there is slow.

**Why**
The album you want to fill is usually the one you're looking at, so starting the import from it is the natural place. Lightroom Classic has the same idea for folders ("Import to this Folder…").

**Proposal**
An **Import ▸** submenu in an album's context menu with the same ways in as File ▸ Import: Import Photos…, Import from Folder…, Import from Device. The import review then opens with that album chosen. `file.addPhotos`, `file.addFolder` and `file.addFromDevice` accept an optional `album` for the same from the CLI and agents.

I have a PR ready.

title: Canon CR2: white level taken from saturated masked rows, so clipped highlights sit at 81 to 96% and are not treated as clipped (EOS 50D, Rebel T1i, T2i, T5, SL1)
author: AlexChambers
body:
## Summary

On `main` at 25ef65c8, the CR2 decoder estimates the white level from the whole sensor buffer, masked borders included. On several bodies the masked rows above the image contain many samples at or near 16383. The plateau search then settles on that strip, or falls back to the full 14-bit range, and misses the image's own saturation plateau. Clipped highlights then normalise to 0.81 to 0.96 instead of 1.0 or more, below the 0.99 threshold that highlight reconstruction and the camera-look fit use to recognise clipped pixels. This is wrong pixels (levels). I found it in a compatibility sweep of the CC0 raw.pixls.us files for every maker except Sony.

title: As-shot white balance not read on six older bodies: Nikon D2H, D50, D70, D70s, Olympus E-10 and Canon PowerShot G9

On `main` at 25ef65c8, six bodies decode from sensor data but come out with no as-shot white balance (`wb_multipliers` is None). While the camera-look fit is accepted the render hides it: four of the six fit, at ΔE76 4.3 to 7.6 against the camera JPEG. title: Nikon: the D1X renders squashed to 3:1 (non-square pixels), the Coolpix E8800 decodes as two stacked fields, and P330/P7700/P7800 NRWs stay preview-only outside #671's layouts
author: AlexChambers
body:
## Summary

On `main` at 25ef65c8, two Nikon NEF layouts decode but give wrong pixels (geometry), and a third stays preview-only without an open PR that covers it. I found all three in a compatibility sweep of the CC0 raw.pixls.us files for every maker except Sony, which covered all 91 Nikon bodies with CC0 files on the site.

## 1. D1X: pixels twice as tall as wide, rendered as if square

| | Value |
|---|---|
| File | [raw.pixls.us 1786](https://raw.pixls.us/getfile.php/1786/nice/Nikon%20-%20D1X%20-%2012bit%2012bit%20uncompressed%20(3.0422960725076).NEF) (12-bit uncompressed) |
| Sensor data | 4028 x 1324, developed 4024 x 1324 |
| Render at `--size 1200` | 1200 x 395, aspect 3.04 |
| Camera preview in the file | 570 x 375, aspect 1.52 (the camera's own JPEGs are 3008 x 2000) |
| Against the preview | luminance correlation 0.20, ΔE76 27.1. The look fit is rejected because the frames don't match. |

The D1X photosites are rectangular, so its 1324 rows cover a 3:2 picture. LightCraft has no notion of a pixel aspect ratio. The DNG `DefaultScale` tag exists as a constant (`crates/tiff/src/tags.rs:118`) but nothing reads it, so DNGs with non-square pixels would be affected too. The compressed D1X NEF stays refused as Huffman-coded (see #671), so only uncompressed D1X files reach this.

Suggested fix (not cheap): give `RawImage` a pixel aspect, set to 2:1 vertical for the D1X and taken from `DefaultScale` for DNG. Then have the develop step resample after demosaicing, so the developed size becomes about 4024 x 2648. A per-model special case in the NEF decoder would also work, but it can't simply duplicate mosaic rows without breaking the CFA.

## 2. Coolpix E8800: the E8400's two-field layout, not covered by #672

| | Value |
|---|---|
| File | [raw.pixls.us 2769](https://raw.pixls.us/getfile.php/2769/nice/Nikon%20-%20Coolpix%20E8800%20-%2012bit%2012bit%20uncompressed%20(4:3).NEF) |
| Sensor data | 3280 x 2454, 12-bit, the same size as the E8400 |
| Render | two squashe…

title: Raw recognition: an uncompressed Leaf Aptus 22 MOS opens as a greyscale image of its mosaic, and the Hasselblad Lunar ARW opens preview-only
author: AlexChambers
body:
## Summary

`lightcraft_raw::probe` (`crates/raw/src/lib.rs:139-214`) misroutes two kinds of CC0 raw.pixls.us files on `main` at 25ef65c8. I found both in a compatibility sweep of the site's files for every maker except Sony.

| File | What happens | Severity |

It renders as the raw mosaic shown as greyscale: dark, sideways, no colour. | wrong pixels |
| Hasselblad Lunar ARW ([4051](https://raw.pixls.us/getfile.php/4051/nice/HASSELBLAD%20-%20Lunar%20-%2012bit%20(3:2).ARW)) | classed OtherTiff, so it opens as the embedded preview ("OtherTiff files are not decoded yet"). | preview-only |

## 1. Leaf MOS with an uncompressed raw IFD0

- IFD0 is the raw itself: 4008 x 5344, one tile, 16-bit, compression 1, PhotometricInterpretation 1 (BlackIsZero), one sample per pixel.

title: Panasonic DC-S1RM2: high-resolution mode RW2 (177 MP) opens preview-only (format 8 with tag 0x0043 = 2)
author: AlexChambers
body:
## Summary

On `main` at 25ef65c8, the DC-S1RM2's standard and in-camera-crop RW2s decode from sensor data. The high-resolution mode file is refused instead and opens as its embedded preview. Severity: preview-only. I found it in a compatibility sweep of the CC0 raw.pixls.us files for every maker except Sony; it is the only Panasonic or Leica variant in the sweep that doesn't decode. The other 377 of 378 Panasonic and Leica RW2, RWL and RAW files, from 119 bodies, render from sensor data.

## Measured

| raw.pixls.us file | Mode | Sensor | Tag 0x0043 | Result |
|---|---|---|---:|---|
| [7724](https://raw.pixls.us/getfile.php/7724/nice/Panasonic%20-%20DC-S1RM2%20-%203:2.RW2) | standard hi-res mode, 3:2, 14-bit | 16296 x 10856 | 2 | preview only: "Panasonic raw format 8 with tag 0x0043 = [2]" |
| [7723](https://raw.pixls.us/getfile.php/7723/nice/Panasonic%20-%20DC-S1RM2%20-%203:2.RW2) | 12-bit burst, electronic shutter | 8152 x 5432 | 1 | sensor, fit accepted |
| 7718 to 7722, 7725 | 2:1, 64:25, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3 crops, live composite | 8152 x 5432 | 1 | sensor, each crop's aspect matches its mode |

## Cause

`crates/raw/src/vendor/rw2.rs:132-143` (`FORMAT8_FIXED`) lists the format-8 tags of unknown meaning, with the values every earlier sample carried. Tag `0x0043` must be `[1]`. A file with any other value is refused by design (module docs, `rw2.rs:51-52`) rather than guessed at.

## Suggested next step (about 2 hours to find out; not a guaranteed cheap fix)

- Decode the 7724 strips (tags 0x0044 to 0x0048) with the existing format-8 strip decoder, ignoring 0x0043.
- Compare the result with the embedded preview: luminance correlation, seams between strips, field order.
- If it decodes cleanly, allow 0x0043 = 2 when the strip geometry adds up to the 16296 x 10856 sensor, and pin the file.
- If it doesn't, keep the refusal and record in the reason what 0x0043 = 2 changes.
- At 177 MP the decode also needs a memory check: about 354 MB of 16-bit samples before demosaicing…

title: Blackmagic lossy CinemaDNG (12-bit DCT tiles under compression 7) fails to import: no decoder and no preview to fall back to
author: AlexChambers
body:
## Summary

On `main` at 25ef65c8, two of the five Blackmagic bodies on raw.pixls.us write frames that LightCraft can't open at all. The import fails with "unsupported raw (JPEG process SOF1 (not lossless Huffman)) without an embedded preview", and the files don't reach the library. Severity: failed import. The other Blackmagic files (Pocket Cinema Camera, Pocket Cinema Camera 6K Pro, URSA 4K) decode from sensor data. I found this in a compatibility sweep of the CC0 raw.pixls.us files for every maker except Sony.

| Body | raw.pixls.us file | Size | Coding |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Pocket Cinema Camera 4K | [4440](https://raw.pixls.us/getfile.php/4440/nice/Blackmagic%20-%20Blackmagic%20Pocket%20Cinema%20Camera%204k%20-%2012bit%20(16:9).dng) | 3.2 MB | DNG 1.2, 4128 x 2176, 12-bit CFA, compression 7, four 1032 x 2176 tiles, LinearizationTable |
| Micro Cinema Camera | [7317](https://raw.pixls.us/getfile.php/7317/nice/Blackmagic%20-%20Micro%20Cinema%20Camera%20-%2012bit%20(16:9).dng) | 1.2 MB | same kind |

Other Pocket Cinema Camera 4K frames on the site (4438, 4354) decode, so the camera writes both codings.

## Cause

- Compression 7 is DNG's lossless-JPEG code, but these tiles are DCT-coded: an extended-sequential frame (SOF1) at 12 bits. That works out to about 2.9 bits per pixel, Blackmagic's lossy "3:1 / 4:1" CinemaDNG.
- The DNG reader passes compression-7 tiles to the lossless decoder (`crates/raw/src/tiffraw.rs:168-179`), which refuses SOF1 (`crates/raw/src/ljpeg.rs:318`).
- `docs/raw-parity.md` lists DNG "lossy JPEG" as decoded. That path (`tiffraw.rs:180-191`) handles 8-bit baseline tiles under compression 34892, not 12-bit SOF1.
- The files carry no preview, so `probe_bytes` (`crates/engine/src/files.rs:139-160`) returns an error and nothing is imported.

## Suggested direction (not cheap)

A 12-bit extended-sequential DCT decoder in pure Rust, either in `ljpeg.rs`'s neighbourhood or in the lossy-JPEG path, plus routing SOF1 tiles under compression 7 to it. …

title: Color Science and Input Profiles (DCP/ICC)
author: mmirandalob
body:
from Reddit: As a former photographer, I have a serious question about your Lightroom alternative (and Premiere/After Effects regarding Log/RAW workflows).

Building a clean-room raw processor in Rust is an impressive engineering feat, but how are you handling Color Science and Input Profiles (DCP/ICC)?

Industry adoption of any RAW converter depends almost entirely on its default color rendering. Proprietary software giants like Phase One (Capture One) or Adobe spend millions on laboratory calibrations, reverse-engineering camera sensors to build custom profiles for skin tones, highlight roll-offs, and color matrices.

Pure math gives a flat, mathematically accurate, but aesthetically unusable image. "Vibe coding" with AI can easily generate code for de-mosaicing (like bilinear or AHD), but AI doesn't have access to custom color science or proprietary camera profiles.

Are you planning to bundle open-source profile databases (like darktable's or RawTherapee's LibRaw/Adobe-compatible DCP parser)?

Or is your AI engine generating its own look-up tables (LUTs) and profiles? If so, how do you simulate accurate or pleasing colors for hundreds of different camera bodies without physical laboratory testing?

Without a solid color science foundation, it’s going to be extremely hard to convince anyone to switch from Adobe or Capture One, no matter how fast the Rust binary is. Curious to hear your thoughts on this!

title: Temp slider: realistic Kelvin values are crammed into the left sixth of the track
author: MarkusFriedel
body:
**What happens now**

On photos with a Kelvin white balance (DNG, and raws whose camera has measured matrices, #730), the Temp slider runs linearly from 2000 K to 50000 K. As Shot on my Nikon Z 6II NEFs (about 4850 K) sits at 6 % of the track and 10000 K at 17 %. Nearly every temperature a photo needs is crammed into the leftmost sixth of the track:

- dragging is coarse: at the default panel width, one point of pointer movement is more than 200 K,
- the right four fifths of the track (17000–50000 K) are rarely useful,
- the knob barely moves between, say, daylight and shade, so the slider says little at a glance.

**What Lightroom does**

Lightroom Classic has the same range (2000–50000 K), but the track isn't linear: **7000 K is in the middle**. I measured knob positions by lining up the Temp knob with the linear Tint slider (−150…+150) in Lightroom Classic:

| Temp | Tint at the same position | Position on the track |
|---|---|---|
| 2000 K | −150 | 0 % |
| 3650 K | −100 | 16.7 % |
| 5400 K | −50 | 33.3 % |
| 7000 K | 0 | 50 % |
| 15000 K | +87 | 79.0 % |
| 20000 K | +106 | 85.3 % |
| 30000 K | +120 | 90.0 % |
| 50000 K | +150 | 100 % |

The left half is linear (100 K per 1 % of the track). The right half grows logarithmically. This model is within 2 % of every measured position:

```
K ≤ 7000:  pos = (K − 2000) / 10000
K > 7000:  pos = 0.5 + 0.5 · ln(1 + (K − 7000) / 1000) / ln(44)
```

**Why it matters**

White balance is one of the most common edits, and on a raw it's usually set by dragging Temp. With the linear track, fine control is hard exactly where it's needed, and Lightroom users' muscle memory ("a bit right of the middle is a bit warm") doesn't carry over.

**Proposal**

Give the slider a value ↔ track position mapping. The Kelvin Temp control (`wb.temp`) uses the curve above. Every other slider stays linear, including the relative Temp slider of JPEGs and raws without camera matrices (`wb.tempRel`, −100…+100, 0 = as shot). The mapping is used for draw…

title: Camera look: the fitted tone curve ignores the JPEG's darkest tones, so deep shadows come out lifted (EOS R6 Mark II, #1021)
author: AlexChambers
body:
The fitted camera look lifts deep shadows, because it never sees the camera JPEG's darkest tones. On photos with a lot of dark area, blacks come out grey and dark hair or clothing looks washed out (#1021).

## Cause (main 25ef65c8)

- `collect_pairs` (`crates/engine/src/camera_preview.rs:569` and `:572`) drops every sensor/JPEG pair whose JPEG luminance is below 0.015 (about L\* 12.9). The tone curve is fitted only above that.
- Below its first knot, `CameraTone::apply` (`crates/pipeline/src/tone.rs:75`) interpolates in a straight line from (0, 0) to that knot. Cameras put a steep toe there, so everything the JPEG shows between black and L\* 13 comes out lighter.
- On the #1021 ISO 500 file (EOS R6 Mark II, 3B0A1089), the first knot lands at scene 0.0125, display 0.0242 (L\* 17.6). 27% of that JPEG is below the 0.015 floor, so about 28% of the frame is rendered on the straight line.

## Measured on that file

These are numbers only, from the reporter's file, which is already shared on #1021. Whole-frame L\* quantiles, default render on main against the embedded camera JPEG (no pixel alignment needed):

| Quantile | 0.1% | 1% | 5% | 10% | 20% | 30% | 50% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Camera JPEG | 1.41 | 2.26 | 3.36 | 5.41 | 9.68 | 13.50 | 19.11 |
| LightCraft | 4.25 | 6.79 | 9.55 | 11.97 | 15.80 | 17.78 | 20.52 |

- The lift covers the bottom 30% and has mostly gone by the median. The darkest 10% averages L\* 9.29 against 3.49.
- It isn't the decoder. The masked pixels average 2048.0 / 2048.3, and the decoder uses 2048. The darkest areas sit about 35 DN above black, so they're real signal that the camera's toe crushes.
- The ISO 51200 file in #1021 shows the same pattern: darkest 10% at L\* 7.86 against 1.41.
- Noise reduction doesn't change it (Color NR 0 to 100 gives the same tone). The open camera-look PRs (#699, #784, #1206) don't touch this file, which already gets the full look.

## Suggested direction

- Fit the toe from the dark pairs too. Kee…

title: Profile panel: show where a raw's starting colour came from (camera profile, per-photo fit, own matrices or fallback)
author: radialmonster
body:
The Profile panel shows the look ("Color" by default), but it doesn't show where a raw's starting colour came from. On #1281 this made it look as if no camera profile was applied to an ILCE-7CR file, when the built-in ILCE-7CR profile was in use. When a raw renders dull, dark or flat, the first question is which path ran, and today the only way to find out is to render the file with `LIGHTCRAFT_PROFILE=1`.

`starting_colour` / `fit_preview` (`crates/engine/src/camera_preview.rs`) already make this choice, so the answer just needs to reach the UI:

- the raw's own colour matrices (DNG and other formats that carry them)
- a look fitted to the camera JPEG, with a camera profile's colour (built in, or local from the camera-profiles folder)
- a look fitted to the camera JPEG, with the photo's own colour
- spectral-sensitivity colour, after the fit was refused
- the tone of a black-and-white camera JPEG
- the neutral fallback, after the fit was refused

Sony's DRO-off tone swap matters too (see #1300), so it could be noted as well.

## Suggestion

- Return a small `ColourSource` value next to the look. It needs to tell built-in and local profiles apart, which `camera_profiles::get` doesn't report yet.
- Show it as one read-only line under the profile name. For example: "Camera colour: ILCE-7CR profile (built in)", "fitted to the camera JPEG", "neutral (camera look refused)", and "DRO tone removed" where that applies.
- Rendering doesn't change, so no `LOOK_VERSION` or render-cache bump is needed. The line has to follow the selected photo and must not show a stale value while a new look is being fitted.

Related: #1207, which also suggests showing which calibration or fallback was used.

title: Export: a 2000 px long edge gives 1999 px on 3:2 photos (2048 → 2047)
author: Mart95Dev
body:
## Summary

Exporting a 3:2 photo with a 2000 px long edge produces a **1999 × 1333** file. The same thing happens with `width=2000`, `shortEdge=1333` and `height=1333`, and with a 2048 px long edge (→ 2047 × 1365). Other sizes are correct.

`lightcraft-cli render` uses the same export path as the Export dialog (`export_photo`), so app exports are affected too.

## Reproduction

Sony ILCE-7M3 raw from raw.pixls.us (`Sony/ILCE-7M3/_DSC0009.ARW`, CC0). Its full-size export is 6000 × 4000.

```
lightcraft-cli render _DSC0009.ARW -o out.jpg --opt longEdge=2000    → (1999×1333)
lightcraft-cli render _DSC0009.ARW -o out.jpg --opt width=2000       → (1999×1333)
lightcraft-cli render _DSC0009.ARW -o out.jpg --opt shortEdge=1333   → (1999×1333)
lightcraft-cli render _DSC0009.ARW -o out.jpg --opt height=1333      → (1999×1333)
lightcraft-cli render _DSC0009.ARW -o out.jpg --opt longEdge=1200    → (1200×800)
lightcraft-cli render _DSC0009.ARW -o out.jpg --opt longEdge=2500    → (2500×1667)
lightcraft-cli render _DSC0009.ARW -o out.jpg --opt longEdge=4000    → (4000×2667)
```

## Pattern

The long edge loses a pixel exactly when the short edge rounds **down**:

| Requested long edge | Exact short edge | Short edge after rounding | Result      |
|---------------------|------------------|---------------------------|-------------|
| 2000                | 1333.33          | 1333 (down)               | 1999 × 1333 |
| 2048                | 1365.33          | 1365 (down)               | 2047 × 1365 |
| 2500                | 1666.67          | 1667 (up)                 | 2500 × 1667 |
| 4000                | 2666.67          | 2667 (up)                 | 4000 × 2667 |
